ai-43465bb556.headline: US tightens AI chip export controls to deter Chinese companies from accessing compute remotely
ai-43465bb556.fulltext:
The Trump administration on Monday is preparing to roll out new export controls on AI chips and data centers outside the U.S., seeking to prevent companies, especially those in China, from getting past U.S. export controls by remotely accessing AI infrastructure located in other countries.
Under the interim rule, the Commerce Department will require companies to get licenses to export, reexport, or transfer AI chips and servers to data centers anywhere in the world if they may provide compute to companies in China or other restricted countries.
The remote-access rules target companies based in the U.S.’s D:5 group of embargoed countries, which includes China, Russia, Iran, North Korea, and 18 others.
The U.S. already has rules requiring chip companies to get a license to ship AI chips to companies based in, or owned by any business in, this group of countries.
“This new control is a logical extension of existing controls,” the interim rule reads. “These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models.”
The move comes days after Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned amid a scandal involving an alleged Chinese spy linked to one of the chipmaker’s customers. The U.S. government has reportedly been wanting to put that customer, Megaspeed, on a special entity list, as it believes the company has been buying thousands of Nvidia chips to provide compute to Chinese businesses to get past existing export-control restrictions.
Reuters reported last week that Chinese AI companies are rushing to secure computing capacity overseas amid fears of tighter restrictions from the U.S.
The rule applies to data centers or any network that can supply over 12 million total processing performance (TPP), an export-control metric the U.S. uses to measure computing power. (Twelve million TPP roughly works out to the max computing power of about 750 Nvidia H100 or H200 chips.) The rule also covers indirect access through go-betweens or brokers, and exporters and data center operators are required to keep an eye on their customers’ ownership structures and activities to ensure they aren’t run by anyone from the D:5 group.
The rule also adds new licensing requirements for chip exports, reexports, or transfer of advanced semiconductors to Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand, and Brazil. The Commerce Department said it had included these as they “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion.” For these countries, however, the license requirements will not apply to chips “destined” for companies based in the U.S.
Existing data center operators providing services that fall under this new rule are required to get licenses within 90 days of the rule coming into effect.
Notably, the rule doesn’t apply to commercial recommendation systems, like those used in e-commerce or social media.
The rule also rescinds the Biden admin’s AI Diffusion Rule from January 2025, which sought to impose country-level limits on exports of advanced AI chips, and restrict transfers of certain powerful AI models. That May, the Trump administration said it would throw out that framework, arguing that it added unnecessary restrictions on U.S. companies and the country’s allies.
“By making these changes, this IFR prevents the use of certain SI items in data centers and at a computing power level that can be used for training or running of advanced SI models,” the rule reads. “Access to such computing power can be used to train and run advanced SI models capable of supporting military- and intelligence-related activities that could threaten U.S. national security or foreign policy interests.”

ai-a258409b95.headline: OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra tackles the Standard Model's toughest math problem on a lattice
ai-a258409b95.fulltext:
OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra tackles the Standard Model's toughest math problem on a lattice
OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra helped produce a proof that could solve a 50-year-old problem in particle physics.
Physicist Nathaniel Craig of UC Santa Barbara, currently a visiting scientist at OpenAI, presented the approach on the OpenAI blog and as a preprint paper. Craig leads the particle theory group at UCSB and is a permanent member of its Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics.
Physicists can simulate parts of the Standard Model, the theory describing all known particles and fundamental forces, on a computer grid called a lattice. That has already led to breakthroughs like calculating the proton's mass from first principles. But putting the full theory on a lattice has been impossible. The weak force, which governs certain types of radioactive decay, treats left- and right-handed particles differently. On simple lattices, this asymmetry creates unwanted ghost particles. Special lattice particles called overlap fermions can filter them out, but for over 25 years, nobody could set their phase correctly.
Craig had a strategy to fix the phase by comparing progressively finer lattices, but couldn't prove it worked in all the cases it needed to cover. GPT-6 Astra turned the idea into a working construction and took the lead on the detailed proof. Lattice field theorists Maarten Golterman, Andreas Kronfeld, and Yigal Shamir reviewed the proof and raised questions that Craig says helped build confidence in the result. He calls the work "much more a beginning than an end" and says a lot remains before realistic simulations are possible.
The result follows a run of AI advances in mathematics that started in January 2026. In May, OpenAI's disproof of Erdős's unit distance conjecture became the first AI proof worthy of math's top journal. Days later, Google Deepmind's AlphaProof Nexus solved nine of 353 open Erdős problems for a few hundred dollars, and by October its results had passed peer review.
The most far-reaching claim came in September, when OpenAI submitted a 166-page proof for the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize Problem and the Clay Mathematics Institute said it had "apparently been settled". The solution remains under review, and mathematicians have questioned whether OpenAI fully understands its own proof. Across the field, mathematicians have mixed feelings as AI keeps cracking unsolved problems.

ai-d584a637a8.headline: India & Nine Other Nations Sign Joint Declaration To Safeguard AI Supply Chains
ai-d584a637a8.fulltext: India and nine other nations have signed a joint declaration to safeguard supply chains and infrastructure that are central to the development and deployment of advanced AI systems. The agreement, called the San Francisco Declaration on the Secure Foundations of Enduring Prosperity, was signed on November 15 at the Pax Silica retreat, which was convened by US under-secretary of state for economic affairs Jacob Helberg. Besides India, the declaration was also signed by representatives of the governments of the US, Australia, Israel, Japan, the Republic of Korea, Qatar, Singapore, the UAE and the UK. “The declaration affirms that economic security is fundamental to national security, sets out the participants’ common understanding of the sensitive technologies and critical infrastructure that underpin super intelligence (or AI) supply chains, and declares that safeguarding them is a shared endeavor,” read a statement by the US state department. For context, the US government refers to AI as super intelligence (SI) after President Donald Trump signed an executive order to rename it. The declaration has termed the protection of two strategic assets – “critical” AI infrastructure and “sensitive technologies” – as a “shared endeavour” essential to the prosperity and independence of participating countries. The document defines sensitive technologies as goods, software, knowledge, components, inputs and means of production used in AI supply chains. The declaration noted that these technologies could provide a military advantage, create undue economic leverage and pose risks if transferred without authorisation or misused. It also defines “critical infrastructure” as the physical and digital systems that support AI supply chains, including ports, terminals, transport, communications and logistics networks, information technology and digital platforms. The declaration adds that disruption, hostile control or unauthorised exposure of data flowing through these systems could cause significant harm. In addition, the signatories also agreed that AI resilience would be “best” achieved through diversified and trusted supply chains and by building trusted capabilities among participants. The declaration also underscored the importance of coordinated efforts to address AI supply chain disruptions and non-market policies that distort the AI market. It also called for protecting private investment and ensuring a level playing field for innovation and growth. To aid this, the declaration also proposed the setting up of working groups across five separate spaces: Pro-innovation policy frameworks AI adoption in key sectors Supply chain cooperation across the AI stack Safe harbours and supply chain security hubs AI security and resilience “We, the undersigned participants,... reaffirming (reaffirm) the importance of cooperation on the enforcement of our respective policies to protect sensitive technologies and critical infrastructure from undue access, influence, or control, as stated in the Pax Silica declaration…,” added the document. The San Francisco Declaration is part of the broader US-led Pax Silica initiative. The framework aims to build secure and resilient supply chains for critical minerals, semiconductors and AI infrastructure. For India, the multilateral platform offers an avenue to coordinate with other economies on AI supply chains and critical infrastructure. This comes as India seeks to expand its domestic manufacturing in semiconductors and advanced computing, while reducing reliance on foreign sources for components and equipment.

indian-startups-0518cee7e0.headline: Indian semiconductor startup raises $24 million in seed funding
indian-startups-0518cee7e0.fulltext:
Indian semiconductor startup raises $24 million in seed funding
Indian semiconductor startup Bharat Semi has raised $24 million in seed funding to develop image sensors with built-in AI, according to a recent TechCrunch report. The all-equity round was led by Info Edge Group, South Park Commons, and Indus Bridge Ventures, with participation from Valour Capital, Micromax, Gaingels, and individual investors.
The New Delhi-based company, nearly five years old, has yet to earn revenue and is still developing its sensors, with initial commercial production targeted for 2027, as per TechCrunch. The startup shared with TechCrunch that it has secured design wins with US defence technology firm General Atomics and India's Kaynes Semicon.
Bharat Semi is building programmable sensors that capture images, process them, and run AI on a single chip, so visual data does not need to be sent to separate processors. Co-founder Vrinda Kapoor told TechCrunch this could cut system costs by at least 70%, and described the aim as moving "from sensors to sense-making solutions". The company is targeting smart homes, industrial automation, surveillance, and aerospace.
It plans to use the funding to grow its engineering team, finish product development, and bring the sensors to market. It will stay fabless, meaning it designs chips but outsources their manufacturing, as per the report.
Kapoor, a South Park Commons fellow who previously worked in healthcare technology, co-founded the company in late 2021 with Vinayak Dalmia, its managing director, who earlier worked at McKinsey and in private equity. Chief technology officer Boyd Fowler previously held the same role at image-sensor maker OmniVision.

india-deep-tech-e27c600c39.headline: US showing openness to co-producing military equipment but must conform to Make in India—Defence Secy
india-deep-tech-e27c600c39.source: Defence BREAKING NEWS | Defence LATEST NEWS | Defence NEWS TODAY | Defence LIVE UPDATES | Defence TRENDING NEWS | – ThePrint
india-deep-tech-e27c600c39.fulltext:
New Delhi: The US government is showing some openness to co-producing military equipment in India instead of selling it directly off the shelf as before, but like every other trusted partner nation, it will also have to conform to the ‘Make in India’ policy, Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh said Monday.
Addressing a media summit in New Delhi, Singh added that while India hopes for a strong defence partnership with the US, it will not focus on any one particular country as it seeks to establish and maintain strategic autonomy.
Responding to a question on whether India was deepening its defence cooperation with the US and, if so, whether its strategic autonomy was being maintained, Singh said, “We are expanding our defence partnerships with many trusted partners.” He cited the India-EU Security and Defence Partnership signed in January this year as an example, and added that India is among the few countries that enjoy good relations with others that are often at odds, including Iran and Israel, and Russia and France. “I wouldn’t say that we are putting too much focus on any one country.”
Addressing India-US ties specifically, the defence secretary said, “We hope to have a strong defence partnership with the US as well. But they will have to come through the same route like everybody else. If they want to sell us platforms, they will have to conform to our Make in India policies.”
Singh also indicated that positive signs were visible on that front, saying, “They have shown some in-principle agreement…in terms of actually doing co-production in India, as against just off-the-shelf buys that characterised their sales in the past.”
Responding to a question on whether the delays in India’s submarine acquisition programme were becoming a strategic vulnerability amid expanded China-Pakistan naval cooperation, especially with China supplying submarines to Pakistan, Singh said—without providing details—that the internal procurement cycle for a “significant increase in underwater platforms” had been completed through two programmes. This is expected to include the proposed purchase of six conventional diesel-electric submarines, which will be built by state-run Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders based on a design by its German partner, ThyssenKrupp Marine Systems (TKMS), under Project-75 (India), or P75(I).
“Both are being examined at the highest level in government. You will hopefully see some good news on that front fairly soon…and it will be a fairly large programme,” he said.
“We will not allow the existing advantages that we have in the naval side vis-à-vis the adversary that you mentioned to slip away,” Singh added. The P75(I) programme is awaiting final clearance by the Cabinet Committee on Security, after which a formal contract will be signed.
Singh holds additional charge as Secretary of the Department of Defence Research and Development in the Ministry of Defence (MoD) and as Chairman of the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO).
On the Mission Sudarshan Chakra programme—under which India plans to establish an air and ballistic missile defence shield system—the defence secretary was asked when it would begin to be implemented and whether both the defensive and offensive weapons and systems required had been identified. A formal report has been prepared for the programme. “The report is ready… Headquarters Integrated Defence Staff is examining it further,” Singh said.
However, the defence secretary underscored that irrespective of the report, to address existing gaps, particularly in areas such as air defence, procurement action has already been initiated on many of them. “It’s not that we’re waiting for the report to get some kind of formal acceptance before we take procurement action on some of those key capabilities that we need.”
He added that this is being done concurrently with ongoing work across the MoD, in association with the services, on Mission Sudarshan Chakra.

global-economics-5ff2781941.headline: Analysis: The Fed's chairman sees an AI revolution coming. Now he has to figure out what it means
global-economics-5ff2781941.fulltext:
Artificial intelligence is about to sweep through the economy. The Federal Reserve is bracing for impact.
"We are at a hinge point in the U.S. economy," Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said at a conference he convened in San Francisco on Monday. But exactly when and how the economy could turn, and what that means for interest rates and inflation, isn't yet clear.
The meeting of Warsh's AI task force saw the new Fed chairman publicly asking the questions Americans will ultimately expect him to answer. He hinted at a few of his private views on whether white-collar workers could soon face massive job losses, but he largely left the speculation to an array of experts he has assembled to advise the Fed.
With the technology racing ahead, Warsh won't be able to put off giving his own answers much longer. AI lab Anthropic plans to price the shares for its initial public offering on Wednesday and could raise as much as $64 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation. Vast spending from AI firms is prompting the Fed to contemplate raising interest rates in December to slow down the rate of price increases as the tech sector heats up the economy.
Meanwhile Americans are souring on some aspects of the technology. The Nov. 3 midterms saw voters enact an array of state-level measures to slow down construction of the data centers that are essential to powering AI.
Warsh moderated three out of four sessions at Monday's event and was involved in selecting the speakers. Among them was one of the few prominent Democrats who was willing to speak out against that anti-data center trend.
It is "a very troubling sign" that so many anti-data center measures passed in the midterms, Gina Raimondo said. She is a former secretary of commerce under President Joe Biden and a former governor of Rhode Island.
Stopping AI "would be very bad for America" and for the people who voted for the measures, Raimondo said.
Warsh didn't say whether he shares that view, and how it would translate into monetary policy isn't exactly clear.
The event was an unusual one for the Fed. The central bank employs a small army of Ph.D. economists who can rapidly weigh in on anything affecting the U.S. and global economies. But in keeping with his longstanding critiques of the Fed as insular and outdated, Warsh has chosen to draw expertise from outside the institution to help it figure out how to think about what AI will do to productivity and jobs.
Warsh has assembled a task force on that issue, alongside four others devoted to aspects of Fed policymaking.
The public heard Monday from one of the three official members of the task force: venture capitalist Marc Andreessen. Warsh went to Stanford University with Andreessen's wife, and the two have been longtime friends. Another task force member, Stanford economist Chad Jones, is on leave and working at Anthropic and couldn't speak during the company's blackout period ahead of the IPO. The third, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma, didn't attend the event.
Andreessen is hugely optimistic about the promise of AI as a technology, but believes the government won't let Americans experience its full effects. Heavy regulation in areas such as healthcare and education mean technology can't replace people's jobs in those sectors, he said.
"To the extent our economy is a free-market economy, then maybe you could see the, let's say, extremely rapid displacement scenarios people are talking about," Andreessen said. "But we've mostly outlawed the kind of job transition that … both the utopians the doomers talk about."
Warsh returned repeatedly to one scenario for the economy that draws on past experience. The so-called China shock unfolded after that country joined the World Trade Organization in 2001 and moved heavily into low-cost manufacturing. Americans saw prices on clothing and furniture drop rapidly, for instance, but at the cost of severe job losses. One widely cited estimate found the U.S. lost a million manufacturing jobs and 2.4 million jobs overall in the years that followed.
Warsh suggested to one of the panelists that the widespread adoption of AI might produce its own version of the China shock, this time focused on service workers.
"I don't want to hold this too tightly," Warsh said. "But if in some ways over the last generation or generation and a half, the China shock, for lack of a better word, lowered prices of goods in the United States, the way that I heard you talking about the philosophy of this new technology is it might do something for services."
In other words, AI could do, say, legal or administrative work more cheaply than a human. That could lower prices but put many people out of a job.
Warsh asked panelists whether "we should expect disinflation over the medium term, from what AI could do to services."
They largely suggested it was possible, which could mean the Fed might eventually want to lower interest rates over the long term.
But at the end of the day, it is Warsh and his fellow Fed members who will need to have conviction on the answer.
There are still many steps between the task force discussion and any kind of change in Fed policy. First, the three task force members will have to assemble their points of view into a report for Warsh sometime in the next few months. Then the Fed itself will need to debate those results and decide whether or how to use them to shape monetary policy.
But with AI growing bigger every day, the Fed may need to make up its mind sooner rather than later.

ai-aae8c4832e.fulltext:
Three months after introducing its product, AI cybersecurity startup Corma has raised a $125 million Series A round at a $1 billion valuation led by NEA, the company said. Corma offers AI models and agents trained for cybersecurity defense. It has now raised a total of $185 million from backers, including Sequoia Capital, Khosla Ventures, and Coatue.
The startup came out of stealth in August. Interest in its product skyrocketed after a series of security incidents sent chief information security officers scrambling on October 21 when a critical flaw was found in PHP, a popular web programming language. Another flaw was found in Node.js, the open source JavaScript runtime environment. Popular open source tool LiteLLM, a proxy for routing requests to multiple LLM providers, also disclosed a security incident. Other incidents were disclosed that day, too. The day showcased the kind of onslaught on security that AI has enabled.
Corma isn’t the only company using AI to play defense. Other examples include Kevin Mandia’s new startup Armadin, as well as Anthropic, OpenAI, Microsoft, and other established players, and too many other startups to count. Still, it’s a young market and a necessary one. Corma says it stands out from the crowd by being a frontier AI research lab focused on protection.

ai-ddcd7a9ae2.headline: AI models ‘weak and fallible’ on climate science, UN-backed study reports
ai-ddcd7a9ae2.fulltext:
Artificial intelligence models can quickly turn into climate crisis deniers at the mildest challenge from users, according to a new UN-backed study.
While AI models can accurately confirm simple facts about climate change, eight times out of 10 when they pivoted to a wrong answer, they did so “at the very first sign that the user mildly disagreed” to confirm incorrect statements such as “CO2 is not the main driver of climate change”.
The report uncovered a strong tendency for AI models to be sycophantic, meaning the model is more interested in pleasing the user than standing by facts – an issue identified when people turn to AI chatbots for personal advice.
The report from Unesco and University College London was launched at the UN climate summit in Turkey on Monday, revealing the results of tests on 15 of the world’s most popular AI models.
Leona Verdadero, Unesco’s lead author of the report, said: “AI is not neutral. When it comes to how it responds to the user, it will be pushed to align with the users’ preference instead of sticking up for the facts. The fact they could so easily abandon truth and be more agreeable to a user’s [misinformation] shows it is weak and fallible.”
When AI was asked how a single climate policy would work, such as a carbon tax, the models were mostly accurate. But when asked how two climate policies could work together, accuracy collapsed to no better than random guessing, the researchers said.
Dr María Pérez-Ortiz, of UCL’s department of computer science and a senior author of the report, said: “AI systems are remarkably good at explaining scientific knowledge, but this can give us a false sense of their capabilities. Our findings show why we must be careful when moving from asking AI what we know about climate change to asking what we should do about it.”
AI models also had a language problem. Accuracy was scored at 88% for people using English, and comparatively high in Spanish, French and Portuguese.
Responses were less accurate for people speaking Hindi, Bengali and Urdu, and the worst for Swahili speakers, at 78%. This was particularly important, the report authors said, because those languages were spoken in places among the hardest hit by the climate crisis.
The report was published on the same day Turkey, the Cop31 host, launched the AI Antalya pledge to make AI “part of the climate solution” with datacentres that are “sustainably” powered.
Julie Cerqueira, of the Natural Resources Defense Council, said AI’s rapid growth was “raising a new set of environmental and existential concerns around the world”.
She said the pledge was an important start but “more work is needed, and it needs to move quickly to keep up with the industry’s rapid-fire development and goldrush mentality”.
Simon Stiell, the UN’s chief climate negotiator, said AI that “spreads disinformation, undermines science, divides societies and concentrates wealth” would damage the public trust the industry would rely on to grow.
“Communities are already pushing back against datacentres, concerned about their water, their energy bills and their environment. So public support is already sinking in deeper underwater,” he said.

indian-startups-fe5da97e00.headline: Dreamteam Bags $53 Mn To Disrupt The CRM Space With AI
indian-startups-fe5da97e00.fulltext: AI-native customer relationship management (CRM) platform Dreamteam, cofounded by former Freshworks executives, has emerged out of stealth mode. The startup has now raised $53 Mn (nearly ₹498 Cr) in a strategic funding round from Together Fund, Accel and Premji Invest. The startup did not elaborate how it plans to utilise the funds. “... CRM is among the biggest software categories ripe for disruption. I've worked alongside Dreamteam's founders since day one as their vision for an AI-native CRM took shape. Their deep CRM expertise and proven record of scaling enterprise software make them uniquely positioned to lead this reinvention,” said Together Fund cofounder and partner Girish Mathrubootham. Founded in 2025 by former Freshworks executives Anand Venkatraman, Ramesh Parthasarathy and Senthil Kanthaswamy, Dreamteam is building an AI-powered CRM platform. Its four AI agents help enterprises track commitments, flag pipeline risks and automate routine sales workflows. The startup claims that its AI platform pulls data and context from customer conversations, emails and Zoom interactions to enable AI coworkers to automate regular work. In addition, it also allows businesses to create custom apps and dashboards using natural language without writing code. Dreamtech claims to already cater to hundreds of companies across industries such as AI, online media, healthcare, manufacturing, and consulting. Going forward, Dreamteam said that it plans to focus on expanding its use cases across the entire customer lifecycle, including prospecting, onboarding and upselling. The fundraise comes amid growing investor interest in Indian AI startups. As per Inc42 data, homegrown AI ventures raised $438 Mn across 35 deals in Q2 2026, up 265% YoY. Venture capital (VC) and private equity (PE) firms remain bullish on startups that help enterprises put AI to work across business functions. Just last month, US-based AI code testing startup Blacksmith bagged $66 Mn in its Series C round led by Sequoia Capital. Prior to this in October itself, another enterprise AI startup AuxoAI also raised $20.7 Mn in its Series A funding round led by NTTVC. Fractal Analytics CEO Srikanth Velamakanni also recently reportedly said that the AI analytics company is in discussions with 20-25 AI startups for potential acquisitions. At the heart of all this is the growing Indian enterprise AI ecosystem, which is projected to become a $71 Bn opportunity by 2030.

Sebi sets up expert panel to review IPO, FPO and capital-raising norms
The Ashish Chauhan-led panel will review eligibility, disclosure, pricing and lock-in requirements under Sebi's ICDR regulations to simplify fundraising and ease market access
Listen to This Article
The Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) has constituted a sub-group of its Primary Market Advisory Committee (PMAC) to review provisions governing initial public offerings (IPOs), follow-on public offers (FPOs), preferential issues and qualified institutional placements (QIPs), with a focus on simplifying regulations and easing access to capital markets for eligible issuers.
The sub-group will review Sebi’s Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements Regulations, 2018. 
The regulator plans to rationalise regulatory requirements, eliminate duplicative disclosures and procedures, and improve regulatory clarity and consistency.
The review will cover eligibility conditions for issuers across different modes of capital raising, lock-in requirements applicable to promoters and pre-issue capital, and application, allocation and allotment mechanisms.
The panel will also examine disclosure requirements in offer documents and other prescribed filings, pricing norms and price discovery frameworks, including determination and disclosure of price bands and floor prices.
The panel is chaired by NSE managing director and chief executive officer Ashish Chauhan. Its members include representatives from BSE, the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India, the Institute of Company Secretaries of India, ICICI Securities, Kotak Investment Banking, Khaitan & Co, S&R Associates, Stakeholder Empowerment Services and CII.
The sub-group may co-opt additional members or invite subject matter experts and stakeholders. Its recommendations will be placed before PMAC for consideration.

indian-startups-24c39ce649.fulltext:
Gurugram-based home services platform Urban Company has opened its qualified institutional placement (QIP) to raise funds from institutional investors, setting the floor price at Rs 161.03 per equity share.
In a regulatory filing, the company said its fundraise committee approved the opening of the issue on November 16, along with the preliminary placement document.
The QIP is part of the company's proposed fundraise of up to Rs 2,500 crore, which was approved by its board on October 16, 2026. Shareholders subsequently cleared the proposal through a special resolution passed via postal ballot.
The floor price has been determined in accordance with the pricing formula prescribed under SEBI's Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements (ICDR) Regulations. Urban Company may offer a discount of up to 5% on the floor price, with the final issue price to be decided in consultation with the book running lead managers.
However, the company has not disclosed the final issue price or the number of shares to be allotted.
The proposed fundraise comes as Urban Company continues to invest in its instant home services business, InstaHelp, amid competition from players such as Snabbit and Pronto. The company has also earmarked a portion of the proceeds for potential inorganic growth opportunities, including acquisitions.
About Rs 1,025 crore (41% of the issue), the largest allocation, has been set aside for inorganic growth opportunities and general corporate purposes. These opportunities could be in India or its existing international markets, including the UAE and Singapore.
The remaining Rs 1,475 crore (59%) will be used to grow its existing businesses. This includes Rs 600 crore (24%) for building the supply ecosystem for InstaHelp, Rs 540 crore (21.6%) for marketing and brand building, Rs 200 crore (8%) for developing technology and platform capabilities, Rs 85 crore (3.4%) for training infrastructure to onboard service professionals, and Rs 50 crore (2%) for research and development of Native products.
In the September quarter of FY27, Urban Company's operating revenue increased 41.4% year-on-year to Rs 537.29 crore. However, its consolidated net loss widened to Rs 182.48 crore from Rs 59.33 crore in the corresponding quarter last year, largely due to investments in InstaHelp.
As of September 30, 2026, the company had Rs 1,901 crore in cash and treasury investments.

india-deep-tech-ad8e88fef3.source: Defence BREAKING NEWS | Defence LATEST NEWS | Defence NEWS TODAY | Defence LIVE UPDATES | Defence TRENDING NEWS | – ThePrint

New Delhi: The Indian Air Force (IAF) expects to receive its first squadron of the crucial indigenous Tejas Light Combat Aircraft (LCA) Mark-1A (Mk1A) jets, whose deliveries have been delayed, by the end of March 2027 at the latest, Chief of the Air Staff Air Chief Marshal Ashutosh Dixit said on Monday.
“Very shortly, we will have LCA [Tejas] Mk1A joining [the] Indian Air Force. Within this financial year, we will have a squadron. Then we will continue developing; we will take it further… LCA [Tejas] Mark-2 will roll out maybe next year. And we are working very hard also for AMCA (Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft),” said the Air Chief Marshal in response to a question at a media summit in New Delhi.
An IAF squadron typically comprises 18 aircraft, and the force has ordered a total of 180 Tejas Mk1A jets. The IAF is currently at its lowest strength in 60 years, with 29 active fighter squadrons against a sanctioned strength of 42.
ThePrint was the first to report last week that the first one or two Tejas Mk1A jets are likely to be handed over to the IAF early in 2027, possibly as soon as January.

— ANI (@ANI) November 16, 2026
Also Read: R&AW is being blamed in Bangladesh for air force pilot’s death. It’s a red herring
Why have deliveries been delayed?
State-run aerospace and defence company Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) missed its original February 2024 deadline to begin deliveries of the first batch of 83 Mk1A jets, contracted in February 2021 for Rs 36,400 crore. The delay was primarily attributed to the late delivery of F404-IN20 engines by US manufacturer GE Aerospace.
The project was also affected by the complex process of integrating weapons and other systems. Deliveries of this first tranche were originally scheduled to be completed by February 2028.
In September 2025, HAL received a second order for 97 Mk1A aircraft, worth over Rs 62,370 crore. Deliveries under this contract are expected to begin in financial year 2027-28 and be completed over six years.
The Mk1A is an upgraded version of the indigenous Tejas Mk1 which is already operational with the IAF. Classified as a 4.5-generation fighter, it is equipped with an active electronically scanned array (AESA) radar, which lets it scan faster, track several targets at once, detect adversaries from longer distances and resist jamming better.
The aircraft is also equipped with beyond-visual-range (BVR) missiles, allowing pilots to engage enemy aircraft from greater distances. Its electronic warfare suite protects it against adversary sensors and weapons.
The Tejas Mk2 is envisaged as a more advanced and heavier variant, powered by more powerful GE engines. However, its prototype has yet to take its first flight.
The AMCA, meanwhile, is India’s stealth combat aircraft under development. It is being pursued through an industry partnership model, and the process of selecting the company or consortium that will help develop and build its prototypes is underway.

U.N. talks seek to rein in 'killer robots' as fears over AI weapons grow
GENEVA — Negotiations on possible rules for the use of lethal autonomous weapons, also known as 'killer robots' are underway at the United Nations in Geneva.
Supporters of controls on autonomous weapons say this week's U.N. conference on Certain Conventional Weapons (or CCW), which meets just once every five years, is the last best chance to agree rules before it is too late.
Warfare technology has advanced rapidly in the last few years, with some experts warning that the world is just months away from having weapons that can choose targets and make the decision to kill autonomously.
In Ukraine and Gaza, AI-assisted weapons have already been used to take out targets, with Ukrainian civilians reporting being 'hunted' by drones as they shop or go to school. But these are still controlled remotely by humans.
Humanitarian organizations say the decision to kill – and responsibility for that choice – must stay in human hands. Ahead of this week's meeting, the United Nations, the International Committee of the Red Cross and the Pope have all called for legally binding rules. U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned that allowing fully autonomous weapons to kill would be 'crossing a moral red line'.
What are the risks?
The Red Cross is especially worried that existing rules of war – the Geneva Conventions – cannot be fully respected by autonomous weapons. War is often chaotic and confusing, and the situation can change rapidly. Under the Conventions, soldiers who are wounded or in the process of surrendering can no longer be targeted.
Georgia Haines, a legal adviser with the Red Cross, worries that autonomous weapons will not be able to distinguish between a soldier who is still fighting, one who is wounded and one who wants to surrender.
'The risk is that, based on the technology we are seeing, they are not able to understand in the same way that a human is the contextual signals. And so the risks are incredibly high that there will be a misidentification of a target.'
Meanwhile, human rights groups warn that the technology behind AI-assisted weapons is becoming increasingly cheap and easy to use. The more it is adopted by the military, the greater the danger of proliferation and its use by terrorist groups or law enforcement agencies in repressive regimes. In theory, a swarm of autonomous drones could be programmed to kill everyone wearing a red sweater, everyone carrying a poster or even everyone speaking a certain language.
Many of the countries now meeting in Geneva take such concerns very seriously. At least 50, including Ireland, Italy, Brazil, Mexico, France and Germany, are calling for a strict timetable to agree on binding rules governing autonomous weapons.
But among states that are already developing and using semi-autonomous weapons, there is pushback. The United States, Russia and Israel have indicated they are set to oppose legally binding rules, with Washington proposing a five-year timetable to draft non-binding guidelines instead.
The U.S. is traditionally a late adopter of international treaties. It did not ratify the Ottawa Convention on landmines, for example, although it did, over time, stop deploying them and reduce its stockpiles.
Under President Trump, doubts about international law have grown. Washington has imposed sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court, and just this weekend, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, in a keynote speech to the Federalist Society, warned against "quoting laws to men with swords."
The problem for states meeting in Geneva is that U.N. negotiations on limiting specific weapons are supposed to be conducted by consensus. This was achieved in 1995, when countries agreed to a ban on blinding lasers, but other agreements have proved elusive. With landmines, countries frustrated by the delay finally took negotiations outside the U.N. process to create the Ottawa Convention.
This week, there may be a compromise: a longer or even open-ended negotiating period to come up with rules that individual states can adopt as binding or non-binding. For diplomats supporting such a solution, it is a way to ensure at least some progress. For campaigners, it is less than ideal, with one likening it to kicking a very dangerous can down the road.

global-economics-9966c77025.headline: What to know about Super Micro Computer as Singapore probes alleged diversion of Nvidia AI servers to China
global-economics-9966c77025.fulltext:
Written By Ravi HariPublished16 Nov 2026, 05:37 PM IST
Super Micro Computer, a US-based server manufacturer whose products are powered by advanced Nvidia artificial intelligence (AI) chips, has come under scrutiny in an investigation into the alleged diversion of billions of dollars' worth of AI servers to China in violation of US export controls.
Three people associated with the company, including co-founder Yih-Shyan (Wally) Liaw, were charged by US prosecutors in March 2026 with allegedly helping smuggle servers containing Nvidia chips worth approximately $2.5 billion to China through Southeast Asia and Taiwan.
The case has acquired fresh significance amid growing scrutiny of how restricted Nvidia AI chips continue to reach Chinese entities despite Washington's export restrictions. It also brings Super Micro back into focus as Singapore investigates companies potentially involved in the diversion of AI servers.
Quick answers to key questions
•5 QUESTIONS
1
What does Super Micro Computer do in the AI chip supply chain?⌵
Super Micro designs and manufactures servers and data-centre systems, including systems that integrate Nvidia GPUs. These servers provide computing infrastructure used to train and run AI models.
2
What are the allegations against Super Micro executives?⌵
US prosecutors allege that three people associated with Super Micro conspired to divert at least $2.5 billion worth of servers containing Nvidia GPUs to China, in violation of export controls. The allegations have not been established in court.
3
How were Super Micro servers allegedly routed to China?⌵
The indictment alleges that servers were ordered through a Southeast Asian intermediary, shipped via Super Micro facilities in Taiwan and then sent onward to China. Prosecutors also allege that repackaging, misleading documents and dummy servers were used to conceal the shipments.
4
Was Super Micro Computer charged in the US server diversion case?⌵
No. The US indictment charged three individuals associated with the company, but did not name Super Micro Computer as a defendant.
5
Why is Singapore investigating Super Micro Computer?⌵
Singapore authorities said they were investigating possible false declarations involving server purchases and related offences. The ministry said Super Micro had provided limited cooperation, while the company said it had been responsive to Singapore authorities.
The latest developments come amid a separate controversy involving Nvidia co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang, whose extra-marital relationships and the investigation surrounding Megaspeed have drawn attention to the broader network of companies allegedly involved in AI chip transactions.
Singapore's Home Affairs Ministry said on November 13 that it had also been investigating Super Micro Computer, but complained that the company had provided only limited cooperation to its probe. Super Micro, however, said it had been responsive to Singapore authorities and had fully cooperated with US and Taiwanese officials.
So, what is Super Micro Computer, what role does it play in the AI chip supply chain, and what are the allegations against its executives?
Super Micro Computer (also known as Supermicro) is a California-based technology company that designs and manufactures high-performance computer servers, storage systems and data centre infrastructure.
Founded in 1993 and headquartered in San Jose, California, the company specialises in servers used for artificial intelligence, cloud computing, enterprise data centres and high-performance computing. It is listed on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol SMCI.
Super Micro is an important player in the AI infrastructure supply chain because it builds servers that integrate powerful graphics processing units (GPUs) manufactured by companies such as Nvidia.
These servers combine GPUs, processors, memory, networking equipment and cooling systems to provide the computing infrastructure required to train and run large AI models.
Nvidia's chips are particularly important because of their ability to handle the massive parallel computing workloads involved in AI development. Companies building AI data centres rely on manufacturers such as Super Micro to integrate these chips into complete server systems.
This relationship has placed Super Micro at the centre of a wider debate over the movement of advanced US-made AI technology to China, where Washington has imposed restrictions on exports of high-performance chips.
The US Justice Department charged three people associated with Super Micro in March 2026 with conspiring to divert at least $2.5 billion worth of servers containing Nvidia GPUs to China in violation of US export control laws.
The three accused are:
- Yih-Shyan 'Wally' Liaw: Super Micro co-founder, board member and then senior vice-president of business development.
- Ruei-Tsang 'Steven' Chang: A Super Micro employee associated with its sales operations.
- Ting-Wei 'Willy' Sun: A third-party broker accused of helping facilitate the transactions.
According to the indictment, the alleged scheme began in or around 2024 and involved routing servers through a Southeast Asian intermediary to conceal their ultimate destination in China.
Liaw was arrested in California on March 19 and subsequently released on bail.
Importantly, Super Micro Computer itself was not named as a defendant in the US indictment. The charges were brought against the three individuals, and the allegations have not been established in court.
According to US prosecutors, the accused used a company based in Southeast Asia as a pass-through intermediary to purchase servers from Super Micro.
The arrangement allegedly involved several steps designed to conceal the identity of the ultimate Chinese buyers.
- Using a middleman: The Southeast Asian company placed orders for servers containing Nvidia GPUs, making it appear that the equipment was being purchased for its own use.
- Routing shipments: Servers assembled in the US were shipped to Super Micro facilities in Taiwan before being delivered to the intermediary in Southeast Asia and subsequently routed to China.
- Concealing the contents: The accused allegedly worked with shipping and logistics companies to repackage the servers into unmarked boxes before they were transported to China.
- Submitting false documents: Prosecutors alleged that executives at the intermediary provided misleading paperwork to the manufacturer to conceal the actual end users.
- Using dummy servers: The accused allegedly used non-working copies of servers to deceive auditors inspecting the intermediary's operations, while the actual equipment was being shipped to China.
The indictment alleged that the scheme resulted in the sale of at least $2.5 billion worth of servers to the Southeast Asian intermediary, with the majority ultimately diverted to China.
Following the charges in March, Super Micro said it was cooperating fully with the investigation.
The company also announced administrative action against the individuals associated with the alleged scheme.
It placed Liaw and Chang on administrative leave and terminated its relationship with Sun.
In its statement, the company said the alleged conduct violated its internal policies and compliance controls, including measures intended to prevent the circumvention of export control laws.
Super Micro also maintained that it had a robust compliance programme and was committed to complying with US export and re-export regulations.
The case has also drawn attention from Singaporean authorities, who are investigating companies suspected of facilitating the movement of restricted AI servers through the city-state.
In a statement on November 13, Singapore's Home Affairs Ministry said it had been investigating several companies since February 2025, including cloud computing firm Megaspeed and US-based Super Micro Computer, over possible false declarations involving server purchases and other related offences.
The ministry said Super Micro had provided only limited cooperation, prompting Singapore to make repeated requests to the US Department of Justice and the FBI for assistance in securing the company's cooperation.
However, Super Micro disputed the characterisation of its response.
A company spokesperson said it had been responsive to Singapore authorities and had fully cooperated with US and Taiwanese officials. The company also said Megaspeed was not, and had never been, a Super Micro customer.
The Singapore investigation is separate from the US criminal case against the three individuals.
The Super Micro case has gained renewed attention amid a wider controversy surrounding Nvidia and the alleged movement of its advanced AI chips to China.
Nvidia co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang has come under scrutiny following reports involving his alleged extramarital relationships, including one with Alice Huang, a former executive of Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed.
Alice Huang has been investigated by Singapore authorities over suspected involvement in transactions involving AI servers potentially routed through the country. US authorities have also reportedly examined whether Megaspeed helped China obtain advanced Nvidia chips restricted under American export controls.
Singapore's Home Affairs Ministry said Alice Huang was investigated for possible offences involving server purchases and alleged inaccurate information provided to investigators. However, it said there was insufficient evidence to establish that she had committed those offences.
US Attorney General Todd Blanche also said the Justice Department had not reached a conclusion on whether Alice Huang was a Chinese spy.
The controversy has raised broader questions about how Nvidia-powered computing infrastructure could reach Chinese companies despite US restrictions, including through overseas data centres and cloud computing services.
The Super Micro case represents another strand of this scrutiny. Unlike the Megaspeed investigation, the US indictment specifically alleges that individuals associated with a US server manufacturer helped divert physical servers containing restricted Nvidia GPUs to China.
The two cases have intensified questions about the effectiveness of US export controls and the role played by intermediaries, server manufacturers and overseas data centre operators in the global AI supply chain.

climate-energy-bfd3d1c2db.fulltext:

The proposal could extend domestic content requirements (DCR) for energy storage systems beyond projects covered by the government’s viability gap funding (VGF) schemes, bringing a wider range of renewable energy and standalone storage tenders under the requirement.
  November 16, 2026 / 17:48 IST  
The government wants more battery energy storage systems (BESS) used in power projects to be made in India. The Ministry of Power has proposed to extend domestic content requirements (DCR) for BESS to more solar, wind and standalone storage projects, over and above those covered under government incentive schemes.
BESS are large battery installations connected to the electricity grid. They store surplus electricity, including power generated when solar and wind output is high, and release it when generation falls or demand rises. This helps manage fluctuations in renewable energy supply and makes it easier to use more solar and wind power.
In a draft notification, the Ministry of Power has proposed changes to bidding rules for solar, wind-solar hybrid, FDRE and standalone battery storage projects. The changes would require battery storage systems used in these projects to meet the government’s domestic content requirements (DCR).
The draft does not specify a new DCR percentage or identify which battery components must be manufactured in India. These details will be issued by the government through subsequent guidelines and orders, ministry officials told Moneycontrol.
The proposal marks a potential expansion of the government’s domestic manufacturing push in battery storage. So far, the requirements have been linked to specific government-supported schemes. A 20% local content requirement, calculated as a share of total project cost, applies to BESS projects under the viability gap funding scheme that is already being offered by the Ministry of Power.
Separately, the Union Cabinet on November 4 approved a minimum 40% DCR for BESS projects supported under a new ₹14,500-crore VGF scheme. The scheme will support 30 GWh of battery storage capacity as part of a wider 92 GWh grid-scale storage programme.
The latest draft is not restricted to projects receiving VGF support. By incorporating DCR into broader competitive bidding guidelines, the government plants to extend the local component manufacturing mandate to storage systems deployed in projects outside these incentive schemes as well.
The draft also proposes making storage mandatory in the solar component of wind-solar hybrid projects, subject to government orders and regulations. For solar projects, procurement would remain possible with or without storage, but procurers would have to comply with government directions mandating storage alongside solar installations.
For standalone BESS projects, developers’ contributions to the Payment Security Fund would become optional. Any contribution would be capped at ₹5 lakh per MWh, with instalments permitted where specified in the request for selection document.
The ministry has invited comments on the proposed amendments until November 25.

Tankers hit in Strait of Hormuz as drone raises alarm at Iraq gas field
Ships struck as US reinforces its military presence in the Middle East, with the aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt arriving in the region.
Fresh attacks on oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and a drone alert at a major gas field in northern Iraq have raised concerns over the security of energy infrastructure across the region, as tensions between the United States and Iran persist despite diplomatic efforts to end their conflict.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said on Monday that two oil tankers had struck naval mines and caught fire while attempting to cross the southern part of the strait through a route Tehran considers unauthorised.
Separately, Iran’s regular navy said another tanker had caught fire and become immobilised after striking a mine in restricted waters east of the strait.
The claims could not be independently verified, and Iranian authorities did not identify the vessels involved.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency separately reported two tanker attacks in the strait on Monday.
In the latest incident, a tanker was disabled and an engine room fire broke out following an attack seven nautical miles (13km) north of Khasab, Oman.
Earlier, the maritime monitoring agency said another tanker had been struck by an unidentified projectile while travelling out of the strait, also causing an engine room fire. No casualties were reported.
It remained unclear whether either incident was connected to the mine strikes claimed by Iran.
The incidents followed a series of attacks on commercial vessels in recent weeks. The United Nations’ International Maritime Organization recorded 136 security incidents involving vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Middle East between March 1 and November 11, including 35 in October alone.
Drone alert at Iraq gas field
The threats to maritime energy shipments came as another security alert raised concerns over energy infrastructure elsewhere in the region.
In Iraq’s semi-autonomous Kurdistan region, warning sirens sounded after a drone flew over the Khor Mor gas field on Monday, Reuters reported, citing two security sources.
There were no immediate reports of a strike or damage from the latest incident.
Production at Khor Mor had already been halted the previous week following a suspected drone attack that sparked a fire and disrupted 2.8 gigawatts of electricity generation, according to United Arab Emirates-based Dana Gas, one of the facility’s operators.
The field is a major source of natural gas for electricity generation in the Kurdish region, making disruptions particularly significant for local power supplies.
It has faced repeated attacks that Iraqi Kurdish officials have blamed on Iranian-backed armed groups.
No group was identified as responsible for Monday’s drone overflight.
The developments came as the US reinforced its military presence in the Middle East, with the aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt arriving in the region.
A US official confirmed its arrival to Al Jazeera on Monday, bringing the number of American aircraft carriers operating in the US Central Command area to three, as tensions with Iran remained high and diplomatic efforts to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz remained stalled.

world-115d73dd03.headline: Five EU states announce plans for immigration ‘return hubs’ in Rwanda
world-115d73dd03.fulltext:
Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”.
The five countries – Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece – are the first to seek to use the EU’s newly agreed returns law that allows people who have exhausted all avenues of appeal against their removal from Europe to be sent to a third country.
In a statement released on Monday the five EU countries said “concrete negotiations with partner country Rwanda will begin for implementation”, saying the scheme would make “an important contribution to further curbing illegal migration, dismantling the business model of smugglers and relieving the burden on our population”.
Officials hope to send 100 people to Rwanda from early next year to test the model. The scheme will apply to adults whose claims to asylum have been rejected or others with no legal right to live in the EU.
In theory, according to diplomatic sources, migrants would stay in a reception centre in Rwanda for a couple of months, before choosing to integrate into life in the Great Lakes country or return to their home nation.
Unlike the failed scheme pursued by the British Conservative government in Rwanda, or Italy’s agreement with Albania, it will not apply to people pursuing asylum claims.
The reception centre, which would be an open facility, was not intended to house people long term but to accommodate regular flows of people, the countries said. Diplomatic sources said the EU countries were not using British-funded facilities built in Kigali.
The governments involved argue it will protect the European asylum system while removing the incentive for irregular migrants to come to Europe.
Denmark’s immigration minister, Morten Bødskov, whose government has pioneered a tough line on migration widely emulated across the EU, said it was “a huge breakthrough”.
The German interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, said: “Return hubs offer a positive approach for people without the right to stay and with no prospects in Europe, whose countries of origin do not cooperate in the repatriation process.”
Andy Burnham told reporters last week that the UK had not had direct discussions with European governments involved in return hubs but “we will watch that with interest, learning from what went on in the past. The public want us to do whatever we can to deal with illegal immigration.”
Critics have highlighted the ethical difficulties of striking an agreement with Rwanda’s repressive government, which was found in 2024 by the US state department to allow state security forces and civilian officials to commit human rights abuses with impunity, while also raising concerns about freedom of expression and forced labour.
Spain’s socialist prime minister, Pedro Sanchez, said on Monday the move had no “future or humanity”. “I don’t see any future or humanity in that. It’s not the solution,” Sanchez, an outspoken defender of immigration in a Europe that has tilted to the right in recent years, told Telecinco television.

other-interests-0b917f2703.headline: Nuclear bomb in space would disable 98 per cent of satellites within a week
other-interests-0b917f2703.fulltext:
A single nuclear explosion in space would wipe out 98 per cent of satellites within a week, sending vital technology around the world into disarray from which it would take years to recover, warn experts.
Zachary Petersen at the University of Wisconsin–Madison and his colleagues modelled the effect of a 1 megaton explosion 500 kilometres above the South Atlantic. They found that an initial spike of X-rays from the blast was damaging, but it wasn’t the most disruptive part: electrons released by radioactive fission would become trapped in Earth’s magnetic field, exposing satellites to a kind of artificial radiation belt, over and over again.
This level of exposure would take out 98 per cent of satellites within one week. And while many spacecraft use specialised computer chips that are more resistant to radiation, the researchers found that even when they altered their simulations to assume that satellites were three times more resilient to radiation damage, the effects were still disastrous, with 97 per cent still failing within two weeks.
Advertisement
Worryingly, such explosions aren’t without precedent. The US detonated a 1.4 megaton nuclear bomb at an altitude of 400 km in 1962. Satellites were disrupted by the blast, but Earth was orbited by only a relatively small number of devices at the time – humans have now launched around 25,000 objects into space, many of which still orbit the planet. Global navigation systems like GPS, internet connections and weather forecasts rely on these satellites and the data they provide.
A nuclear explosion in space would probably have long-lasting repercussions, not only because satellites would need to be replaced, but because there would be an estimated 20 collisions within two years as broken satellites drifted aimlessly. Those collisions present a risk of Kessler syndrome, a theoretical scenario in which debris hits other satellites, creating more debris and a chain reaction of destruction that would make orbit lethal to future launches for decades, or even longer.
The Outer Space Treaty now bans the launch of nuclear weapons into space, and all major spacefaring nations are party to it. But tensions remain. In 2024 a vote was raised at the UN to reaffirm commitment to the rule, which Russia vetoed. Earlier that year, the US had warned that Russia plans to launch a space weapon with possible nuclear capabilities.
Petersen and his colleagues didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment, but Craig Underwood at the University of Surrey, UK, says the consequences of losing so many of our satellites would be catastrophic for society because we are so dependent on space technology.
“The recent low-Earth orbit mega constellations [like Starlink] would be particularly affected,” says Underwood. “During the Cold War, much thought was given to protecting critical space systems and our societies were much less dependent on electronic technology. I suspect that since the 1990s, less attention has been paid to the prospect of having to survive a nuclear conflict. Our civil defence infrastructure has been dismantled, and society is much more vulnerable.”
“While individual satellites can, in principle, be replaced relatively quickly, recovery would not be straightforward. New satellites would have to be launched into an environment still affected by elevated radiation levels and increased debris, potentially limiting their operational lifetime and effectiveness. As a result, restoring orbital infrastructure could take years,” says Chantal Cappelletti at the University of Nottingham, UK. “The result would not be an immediate collapse of modern society, but rather a prolonged degradation of many services that we now take for granted. Recovery would likely require years of rebuilding orbital infrastructure while managing elevated radiation and debris hazards.”

indian-startups-04ef771ca5.headline: India & Nine Other Nations Sign Joint Declaration To Safeguard AI Supply Chains
indian-startups-04ef771ca5.fulltext: India and nine other nations have signed a joint declaration to safeguard supply chains and infrastructure that are central to the development and deployment of advanced AI systems. The agreement, called the San Francisco Declaration on the Secure Foundations of Enduring Prosperity, was signed on November 15 at the Pax Silica retreat, which was convened by US under-secretary of state for economic affairs Jacob Helberg. Besides India, the declaration was also signed by representatives of the governments of the US, Australia, Israel, Japan, the Republic of Korea, Qatar, Singapore, the UAE and the UK. “The declaration affirms that economic security is fundamental to national security, sets out the participants’ common understanding of the sensitive technologies and critical infrastructure that underpin super intelligence (or AI) supply chains, and declares that safeguarding them is a shared endeavor,” read a statement by the US state department. For context, the US government refers to AI as super intelligence (SI) after President Donald Trump signed an executive order to rename it. The declaration has termed the protection of two strategic assets – “critical” AI infrastructure and “sensitive technologies” – as a “shared endeavour” essential to the prosperity and independence of participating countries. The document defines sensitive technologies as goods, software, knowledge, components, inputs and means of production used in AI supply chains. The declaration noted that these technologies could provide a military advantage, create undue economic leverage and pose risks if transferred without authorisation or misused. It also defines “critical infrastructure” as the physical and digital systems that support AI supply chains, including ports, terminals, transport, communications and logistics networks, information technology and digital platforms. The declaration adds that disruption, hostile control or unauthorised exposure of data flowing through these systems could cause significant harm. In addition, the signatories also agreed that AI resilience would be “best” achieved through diversified and trusted supply chains and by building trusted capabilities among participants. The declaration also underscored the importance of coordinated efforts to address AI supply chain disruptions and non-market policies that distort the AI market. It also called for protecting private investment and ensuring a level playing field for innovation and growth. To aid this, the declaration also proposed the setting up of working groups across five separate spaces: Pro-innovation policy frameworks AI adoption in key sectors Supply chain cooperation across the AI stack Safe harbours and supply chain security hubs AI security and resilience “We, the undersigned participants,... reaffirming (reaffirm) the importance of cooperation on the enforcement of our respective policies to protect sensitive technologies and critical infrastructure from undue access, influence, or control, as stated in the Pax Silica declaration…,” added the document. The San Francisco Declaration is part of the broader US-led Pax Silica initiative. The framework aims to build secure and resilient supply chains for critical minerals, semiconductors and AI infrastructure. For India, the multilateral platform offers an avenue to coordinate with other economies on AI supply chains and critical infrastructure. This comes as India seeks to expand its domestic manufacturing in semiconductors and advanced computing, while reducing reliance on foreign sources for components and equipment.

agritech-2f79fb932d.headline: Sebi panel to review IPO, FPO and QIP rules, rationalise disclosure norms
agritech-2f79fb932d.fulltext:
The Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) has set up a panel to review regulations governing public fundraising, including initial public offerings (IPOs), further public offers (FPOs), preferential issues and qualified institutional placements (QIPs), as the market regulator looks to simplify requirements and improve access to capital markets.
The regulator has constituted a sub-group of its Primary Market Advisory Committee (PMAC) to review Chapters II, IIA, IV, V and VI of the Sebi (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018, it said in a statement on Monday. The panel's mandate includes examining issuer eligibility criteria, lock-in requirements, application and allotment procedures, disclosure norms, pricing frameworks and due diligence requirements.
Mint was the first to report on 19 October that Sebi was looking to form the working group. The regulator sent an email to PMAC members on 12 October, inviting nominations until the evening of 13 October. According to the email, the decision to constitute the sub-group was taken at a PMAC meeting held on 12 August at NSE Exchange Plaza.
The review aims to identify ways to facilitate access to capital markets for eligible issuers while rationalising regulatory requirements, eliminating duplicative disclosures and procedures, and improving clarity and consistency, the regulator said. Introduced in 2018 to replace the earlier 2009 framework, the ICDR regulations prescribe the conditions and procedures companies must follow to raise capital through public issues and other routes.
Chapter II covers mainboard IPOs, including issuer eligibility, pricing, promoters' contribution and lock-in requirements. Chapter IV governs FPOs, through which listed companies can raise additional capital from the public. The proposed review comes amid Sebi's broader examination of regulations governing public fundraising.
On 14 October, the regulator reviewed provisions relating to IPOs by small and medium enterprises (SMEs), proposing changes to the listing framework. In a consultation paper, Sebi proposed that companies with a post-issue market capitalization of up to ₹1,000 crore should list exclusively on the SME platform.
Those valued between ₹1,000 crore and ₹4,000 crore could be allowed to choose between the SME and mainboard segments, subject to stricter financial reporting requirements, including the adoption of Indian Accounting Standards, where applicable. The regulator has also proposed raising the minimum average operating profit requirement for SME IPOs to ₹3 crore annually over the preceding three financial years, calculated on restated consolidated financial statements.
The existing requirement is ₹1 crore in at least two of the previous three years.
