Tankers hit in Strait of Hormuz as drone raises alarm at Iraq gas field
Ships struck as US reinforces its military presence in the Middle East, with the aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt arriving in the region.
Fresh attacks on oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and a drone alert at a major gas field in northern Iraq have raised concerns over the security of energy infrastructure across the region, as tensions between the United States and Iran persist despite diplomatic efforts to end their conflict.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said on Monday that two oil tankers had struck naval mines and caught fire while attempting to cross the southern part of the strait through a route Tehran considers unauthorised.
Separately, Iran’s regular navy said another tanker had caught fire and become immobilised after striking a mine in restricted waters east of the strait.
The claims could not be independently verified, and Iranian authorities did not identify the vessels involved.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency separately reported two tanker attacks in the strait on Monday.
In the latest incident, a tanker was disabled and an engine room fire broke out following an attack seven nautical miles (13km) north of Khasab, Oman.
Earlier, the maritime monitoring agency said another tanker had been struck by an unidentified projectile while travelling out of the strait, also causing an engine room fire. No casualties were reported.
It remained unclear whether either incident was connected to the mine strikes claimed by Iran.
The incidents followed a series of attacks on commercial vessels in recent weeks. The United Nations’ International Maritime Organization recorded 136 security incidents involving vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Middle East between March 1 and November 11, including 35 in October alone.
Drone alert at Iraq gas field
The threats to maritime energy shipments came as another security alert raised concerns over energy infrastructure elsewhere in the region.
In Iraq’s semi-autonomous Kurdistan region, warning sirens sounded after a drone flew over the Khor Mor gas field on Monday, Reuters reported, citing two security sources.
There were no immediate reports of a strike or damage from the latest incident.
Production at Khor Mor had already been halted the previous week following a suspected drone attack that sparked a fire and disrupted 2.8 gigawatts of electricity generation, according to United Arab Emirates-based Dana Gas, one of the facility’s operators.
The field is a major source of natural gas for electricity generation in the Kurdish region, making disruptions particularly significant for local power supplies.
It has faced repeated attacks that Iraqi Kurdish officials have blamed on Iranian-backed armed groups.
No group was identified as responsible for Monday’s drone overflight.
The developments came as the US reinforced its military presence in the Middle East, with the aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt arriving in the region.
A US official confirmed its arrival to Al Jazeera on Monday, bringing the number of American aircraft carriers operating in the US Central Command area to three, as tensions with Iran remained high and diplomatic efforts to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz remained stalled.

world-8d5a143784.headline: Five EU countries announce migrant deportation centre in Rwanda
world-8d5a143784.fulltext:
Five EU countries announce migrant deportation centre in Rwanda
- Published
Five EU countries will open a migrant deportation centre in Rwanda next year as part of a broader push to boost removals.
Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands are expected to open a "return hub" ready to accept transfers in 2027, the Dutch and Danish governments announced in statements.
The countries said the scheme would apply to migrants staying illegally in their nations who are subject to deportation, with the Dutch government adding it will provide an alternative if deportees cannot be returned to their country of origin.
Deportees will be able to either integrate into Rwandan society or return to their home country, the nations said.
The scheme will apply to people who have exhausted their legal avenues to stay in the five nations - unlike a scrapped British deal that envisaged sending people to Rwanda to have their claims processed. Legal challenges meant the UK deal never took off, and it was eventually junked by the incoming Labour government in 2024.
Downing Street has not ruled out the UK joining the scheme, saying they will watch it "with interest".
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said the plan to open a centre in Rwanda had no "future or humanity", according to AFP news agency.
"I don't see any future or humanity in that. It's not the solution," Sanchez told the Spanish broadcaster Telecinco, AFP reported.
The five countries say the plan to send migrants abroad is in line with EU and international law, but human rights bodies say it could violate migrant rights.
The deal follows a recent EU reform that allowed for the creation of hubs outside of the bloc.
In a joint press conference in Vienna on Monday, Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker said the five countries wanted to relieve European asylum systems and stop traffickers arranging deadly trips across the Mediterranean.
In a written statement, the Dutch government said the five countries will "only return single men" as part of the first phase of the deal, adding that the focus for the Netherlands "will be on persons from countries of origin in the same region as Rwanda".
Once in Rwanda, people will be able to integrate into society, which means they will have the right of residence, as well as access to education, healthcare, the labour market and the legal system.
Rwandan Interior Minister Vincent Biruta said the country is commmited to working with European partners to provide a "safe, legal and dignified solution for migrants".
He added that they would also work on "correcting the global imbalance in economic opportunities", which he called a "key driver of irregular migration".
Ahead of the announcement, diplomatic sources told the AFP news agency the hub is expected to initially run as a pilot, hosting about 100 people, with each of the five nations possibly sending about 20 migrants.
The United Nations' International Organisation for Migration (IOM) could play an ancillary role.
"IOM has a long history of providing assistance to migrants in situations of transit, including in complex contexts," an IOM spokesperson said, adding the agency was in discussions with some EU countries "on plans for the establishment of return hubs or similar mechanisms".
With elections approaching in several EU nations, administrations have been under pressure to show they can control migration.
Concerns around security, struggling economies and disillusionment with governing parties have all had a major role in shaping attitudes towards people leaving their home countries.
Human Rights Watch's senior Africa researcher Clementine de Montjoye said the choice of Rwanda would be a cause of concern as it had a "well-established record of repression of dissent, arbitrary detention, ill-treatment in detention" and support for armed rebels in the neighbouring Democratic Republic of Congo.
"Paying Kigali to host a deportation programme would not only cause suffering and harm to those deported, it would finance and provide political leverage to a government responsible for serious human rights abuses at home and abroad."
The independent EU Agency for Fundamental Rights argued any third country hosting a return hub should "respect fundamental rights", including that people should not be sent to a country where they face serious risk of persecution.
The agency added that unaccompanied children should not be sent to a return hub, which the Dutch government has confirmed will not take place.
According to the European Border and Coast Guard Agency, there were almost 110,000 irregular border crossings into the EU in the first 10 months of 2026, which represents a 29% decrease compared to the previous year.
In October, about 18,100 crossings were detected, which is about 6% less than October 2025 but 22% more than in September "largely because of a sharp rise in arrivals on the Western African route to the Canary Islands".

global-economics-af65610e26.headline: India joins US-led AI supply chain alliance: Can it break China's grip on AI and semiconductor supply chains..
global-economics-af65610e26.fulltext:
India has taken another step towards securing its position in the global artificial intelligence economy by signing the San Francisco Declaration on the Secure Foundations of Enduring Prosperity on November 15, 2026. The agreement, adopted by India, the United States and eight other governments at the Pax Silica Founders Retreat in San Francisco, seeks to strengthen international cooperation in protecting the technologies, industrial resources and infrastructure essential for advanced AI systems.The declaration brings together the United States, India, Australia, Israel, Japan, South Korea, Qatar, Singapore, the United Arab Emirates and the United Kingdom. It recognises that economic security and national security are increasingly interconnected, particularly when access to semiconductors, critical minerals, computing infrastructure and energy systems can determine a country's technological and strategic capabilities.India's participation is significant because the global competition over AI is extending beyond software development and advanced algorithms. Countries are increasingly concerned about who controls semiconductor manufacturing, rare-earth processing, specialised equipment, data centres and the infrastructure required to sustain large-scale computing. The declaration reflects an effort to develop trusted international supply chains that are less vulnerable to geopolitical disruptions and concentrated industrial dependencies.The Indian delegation was led by S. Krishnan, Secretary, Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY). Krishnan also participated in a discussion titled "India's Place in the Global AI Race" at the Pax Silica Global Leaders Meet on November 15. The discussion focused on India's growing contribution to AI innovation, international technology partnerships and the development of trusted AI systems.Krishnan's involvement represents continuity in India's engagement with Pax Silica. He signed India's initial Pax Silica agreement in February 2026, in the presence of Union Electronics and IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw. During evidence before Parliament's Committee on External Affairs in March, Krishnan confirmed his role, stating: "The agreement was duly signed, and on behalf of the Government of India, I signed the agreement." His participation in San Francisco therefore forms part of an ongoing government effort to integrate India's semiconductor and AI programmes with international technology partnerships.The declaration proposes five working groups covering innovation-friendly policies, AI adoption, supply-chain cooperation, secure industrial hubs and infrastructure resilience. These mechanisms could provide India with opportunities to coordinate investments, identify vulnerabilities and establish partnerships across different stages of semiconductor and AI production. However, the declaration remains a political commitment. It does not immediately establish binding procurement requirements, technology-transfer obligations or new Indian regulations.For India, the most important challenge is its dependence on foreign suppliers, particularly China, across several segments of the electronics and critical-minerals supply chains. China occupies a dominant position in rare-earth processing and important industrial materials used in advanced manufacturing. India also depends on overseas suppliers for sophisticated semiconductor fabrication equipment, advanced chips and specialised electronic components. These dependencies create vulnerabilities that cannot be eliminated simply by joining an international coalition.The distinction between reducing dependence on China and achieving technological self-reliance is important. Diversifying imports towards Japan, South Korea, the United States and other partners could improve supply security, but would not automatically create indigenous manufacturing capabilities. India needs domestic expertise in semiconductor materials, equipment, advanced packaging, chip design and critical-mineral processing. Pax Silica could facilitate such development if its members move beyond policy coordination towards joint investments, technology partnerships and industrial capacity creation.India's semiconductor programme provides a foundation for this approach. According to MeitY's November 6 announcement, 12 semiconductor projects have been approved across six states, involving investments exceeding ₹1.64 lakh crore. The government has also launched the Semicon 2.0 application portal to support the next phase of semiconductor ecosystem development. The programme seeks to strengthen domestic capabilities in manufacturing, materials, equipment and design.The San Francisco Declaration could complement these initiatives by improving access to technology partners and creating more predictable supply chains. Yet significant challenges remain. Advanced semiconductor manufacturing requires expensive equipment, specialised chemicals, reliable electricity, skilled engineers and sustained research investment. International partnerships can support these requirements, but commercial viability and technological competitiveness will ultimately determine whether manufacturing capacity develops in India.There is also a geopolitical dimension. Pax Silica is emerging amid intensifying technological competition between Washington and Beijing. India has an interest in reducing strategic dependencies on China, but it must also preserve flexibility in its economic and diplomatic relationships. Participation in a US-led technology coalition should therefore be assessed through India's industrial and national-security interests rather than viewed solely as geopolitical alignment.The declaration's practical importance will become clearer when the proposed working groups begin producing concrete outcomes. For India, measurable progress would include semiconductor technology partnerships, investments in critical-mineral processing, access to advanced computing infrastructure and greater participation by Indian companies in trusted international supply chains.The involvement of Secretary S. Krishnan places MeitY at the centre of this emerging technology diplomacy. The ministry's challenge will be to connect international commitments with India's domestic semiconductor, electronics and AI programmes while coordinating with other ministries responsible for minerals, energy, commerce and strategic industries.India has secured a place in an important international conversation about the future of AI infrastructure. The next test is whether that diplomatic engagement can accelerate domestic manufacturing, reduce concentrated supply-chain risks and strengthen India's technological capabilities. The success of Pax Silica, from India's perspective, will be measured less by the declaration itself than by the industrial partnerships and capabilities that follow.

Evidence gathered so far indicates she was likely an intelligence asset, someone who shared information, rather than a fully trained spy, the sources said.
The uncertainty has divided investors over Huang's future and complicated the board’s search for a successor. Nvidia shares fell 3.7% on Monday, a day before the chipmaker is due to report third-quarter earnings.
The "Stand With Jensen" campaign listed SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney among its signatories.
The campaign website showed more than 8,800 signatories identified themselves as current Nvidia employees and more than 94,000 as shareholders, though it cautioned that professional affiliations were self-reported and had not been independently verified.
"We are current and former NVIDIA employees, partners, shareholders, and supporters. We write with gratitude for Jensen Huang and with a clear demand to the Board: bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts," an open letter on the website said.
Huang stepped down on Thursday after reports of alleged affairs with employees, including one who reported directly to him, plunging the AI chip heavyweight into crisis and sending shockwaves through an industry he helped bankroll.
“I think he learned a big lesson,” Trump said on Monday. Trump's reported trades this year suggest he held between $13 million and $62 million in Nvidia stock as of the end of August, the Washington Post reported on Monday, citing a review of his financial disclosures.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, though, has called for Nvidia to appoint an outsider as its next CEO, saying the company needs a "dramatic shake-up" following Huang's departure.
Institutional investors too may prove harder to persuade. Richard Windsor, an independent technology researcher, said he expected large institutional Nvidia investors to oppose Huang’s return while investigations remained unresolved because of the legal exposure and uncertainty it could create.
“They’re very risk-averse,” Windsor said, but he added that his own view was that Nvidia shareholders would ultimately be better served by Huang’s return because of the relationships he has built with the company’s customers and suppliers, particularly TSMC, which manufactures Nvidia’s most advanced chips.
Nowhere is Huang’s unusual reach more visible than in Taiwan, where he was born and where Nvidia relies on TSMC and a sprawling network of suppliers to manufacture the chips and systems underpinning the AI boom.
Born in the historic capital of Tainan before moving to the United States as a child, Huang gradually gained celebrity-like status on the island, where the wave of adulation surrounding him has been dubbed “Jensanity.”
For many Taiwanese, Huang's exit marks the loss of a charismatic champion who helped put the island at the heart of the global artificial intelligence boom, with his influence extending well beyond the technology industry.
Jimmy Yang, 42, who works in marketing, said Huang's departure was a loss for Taiwan, where his influence had extended to local businesses and tourism, and Yang expressed hope that Huang could eventually return to Nvidia, drawing a parallel with Apple co-founder Steve Jobs, who returned to the company after being forced out.
"His private life is his own choice," Yang said. "But whether it's the night market economy he's driven or his help for the tech industry, it has been massive."

Bobins Vayalil AbrahamUpdated17 Nov 2026, 07:30 AM IST Amid reports that ousted CEO Jensen Huang is in talks with close allies about a potential return to the helm of the world's second-most valuable company, the Nvidia board said it is focused on its investigation into the co-founder’s ties to an alleged Chinese spy. Citing unnamed sources, CNBC reported on Monday that Nvidia’s board of directors had not discussed bringing back Huang, who announced his resignation on 12 November. Last week, Nvidia’s board announced that it had hired law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to investigate whether company secrets or national security were compromised, after Huang admitted to having an affair with Alice Huang, a Singapore-based Chinese business executive. On Friday, the board said it was still selecting a search firm to find a new CEO for the company, adding that it had not formally engaged any potential candidates. However, the Financial Times reported that Nvidia’s board has approached the CEO of British chipmaker Arm Holdings, Rene Haas, in its search for a potential successor to Huang. Quick answers to key questions •5 QUESTIONS 1 What is Nvidia's board investigating regarding Jensen Huang?⌵ The board hired law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to investigate Huang’s ties to Alice Huang and whether company secrets or national security were compromised. 2 Has Nvidia's board discussed bringing Jensen Huang back as CEO?⌵ The board has not discussed bringing Huang back, according to reports cited in the article. It said speculation about individual candidates was premature. 3 Who is Nvidia's interim CEO while the board searches for a successor?⌵ Nvidia CFO Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO while the board searches for a new chief executive. 4 How is Nvidia's board conducting its CEO search?⌵ The board said it was still selecting a search firm and had not formally engaged potential candidates. A report said it had approached Arm CEO Rene Haas, but the board described candidate speculation as premature. 5 Why is Nvidia's investigation relevant to the CEO succession?⌵ The board is investigating whether company secrets or national security were compromised. The article says the board is focused on that inquiry while its search for a new CEO continues. Haas, who has led the SoftBank-backed British chipmaker since 2022, worked at Nvidia for around seven years more than a decade ago. He is also understood to maintain professional relationships with Huang and several members of Nvidia's board. "Any speculation regarding individual candidates, whether internal or external, is premature," the board said in a statement. The development comes even as 63-year-old Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and led it for more than three decades, continues to gain support for a potential comeback. US President Donald Trump, a close ally of Huang, said on Monday that he is open to him returning as CEO of Nvidia. According to Trump, Huang “learned a big lesson” and that there is a “big group of people that would like him to return.” Trump also downplayed the scandal. “Nobody’s proven that she’s a spy. She may not be a spy,” he said. Trump suggested that more investigation was needed. But he added that “any woman coming to the country — that’s a beautiful woman that comes from China — they say she’s a spy.” Several tech executives, including Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, have also expressed support for Huang's reinstatement. Nvidia, in the meantime, is led by chief financial officer Colette Kress as the interim CEO.
